gloss: redeem, buy back as next of kin; kinsman-redeemer, avenger of blood; (a second verb) defile, stain
summary: To act as the next of kin: to buy back a brother's land or a brother sold for debt, to redeem a thing vowed to Yahweh, to take the widow and raise up the dead man's name, and to avenge a kinsman's blood; the participle גֹּאֵל is the kinsman who has that right and duty (Lev 25:25; Rut 4:4–6; Num 35:19). Yahweh calls himself Israel's גֹּאֵל, who redeemed them from Egypt and Babylon and will redeem them from death and the grave (Exo 6:6; Isa 44:6; Hos 13:14), and Job's “I know that my redeemer lives” looks to seeing God in his flesh at the last (Job 19:25–26). The noun גְּאֻלָּה is redemption and the right to it. A second verb of the same spelling, in late books, is to defile or stain: blood-stained hands and garments, polluted bread on the altar, priests put out of the priesthood as defiled (Isa 59:3; Mal 1:7; Ezr 2:62).

words.gloss: redeem, buy back; act as kinsman; avenge blood; (niphal) be redeemed
words.summary: About a hundred times, almost all qal, with eight niphal. The qal participle גֹּאֵל is the kinsman, “near to him” (Lev 25:25), “of the remnant of his flesh, of his family” (Lev 25:49), whose part is to restore what a brother has lost; when there is none, the right passes to the next (Rut 3:12) or the man redeems himself (Lev 25:26, 49). Its partner is פָּדָה “ransom” (Jer 31:11; Hos 13:14), and with God as subject it is joined to “save” (Isa 49:26; 60:16). No cognate outside Hebrew is certain: the Jewish Aramaic verb is taken from the Hebrew, and the Peshitta writes ܦܪܩ (Rom 11:26).

stems.gloss: redeem, buy back; act as next of kin; avenge; (participle) kinsman, redeemer, avenger

senses.gloss: buy back land, a house or a kinsman sold
senses.definition: Of the next of kin, or the seller himself: to buy back what a man has sold under need, a field, a house, or himself sold as a servant, so that it returns to the family.

evidence.note: “If your brother becomes poor and sells some of his possession, then his redeemer who is near to him shall come וְגָאַל אֵת מִמְכַּר אָחִיו”: buy back what his brother sold.
“If a man has no גֹּאֵל, and he himself becomes able and finds enough for its redemption.”
Of the Levites' houses: what one of the Levites redeems goes out in the jubilee.

A man sold to a stranger: “one of his brothers may redeem him, or his uncle, or his uncle's son … or any of the remnant of his flesh, of his family, may redeem him; or if he is able, he may redeem himself.”
Boaz offers the nearer kinsman Naomi's field: “If you will redeem it, redeem it … for there is none to redeem it besides you, and I am after you.” “I will redeem it.”
“I cannot redeem it for myself, lest I mar my own inheritance; גְּאַל־לְךָ אַתָּה אֶת־גְּאֻלָּתִי.”

senses.gloss: redeem a thing vowed or tithed
senses.definition: To take back for oneself, at the priest's valuation and a fifth more, an unclean animal, a house, a field or a tithe that has been vowed or given to Yahweh.

evidence.note: Of a vowed animal: “if he will indeed redeem it, he shall add a fifth to your valuation.”
“If he who sanctified it will redeem his house.”
Of a field sanctified to Yahweh.
“If a man will indeed redeem any of his tithe, he shall add a fifth to it.”

senses.definition: The participle גֹּאֵל as a noun: the near relative who has the right and duty to redeem, and in Ruth to take the widow and raise up the dead man's name on his inheritance.

evidence.note: “The man is near to us (קָרוֹב לָנוּ); he is one of our redeemers (מִגֹּאֲלֵנוּ).”
“Spread your skirt over your handmaid, for you are a גֹּאֵל.”
“It is true that I am a גֹּאֵל; yet there is a גֹּאֵל nearer than I.”
“Behold, the גֹּאֵל of whom Boaz had spoken passed by.”
The women to Naomi of the child Obed: “Blessed be Yahweh, who has not left you this day without a גֹּאֵל.”
“If the man has no גֹּאֵל to whom the guilt payment may be restored”: the next of kin who receives what was owed to the dead.
Zimri killed all the house of Baasha, “his kinsmen (וְגֹאֲלָיו) and his friends”.

senses.definition: גֹּאֵל הַדָּם: the kinsman of a man killed, whose part is to put the killer to death; the cities of refuge shelter one who killed unawares from him until judgment.

evidence.note: “גֹּאֵל הַדָּם, he shall put the murderer to death; when he meets him, he shall put him to death.”
“The cities shall be to you for refuge from the גֹּאֵל, that the killer not die until he stands before the congregation for judgment.”
“Lest the avenger of blood pursue the killer while his heart is hot.”
“They shall be your refuge from the avenger of blood.”
“Let the king remember Yahweh your God, that the avenger of blood not multiply destruction.”
The king “shall redeem their soul from oppression and violence, and precious shall their blood be in his sight”: redeem and blood together.

senses.definition: Yahweh acts as Israel's next of kin: he brought them out of Egypt, will bring them out of Babylon and from among the nations, and calls himself their Redeemer; those he brings back are “the redeemed of Yahweh”.

evidence.note: “I will bring you out … and deliver you from their slavery, וְגָאַלְתִּי אֶתְכֶם with an outstretched arm and with great judgments.”
“You led in your kindness the people whom you redeemed (גָּאָלְתָּ).”
“Remember your congregation which you bought of old, which you redeemed, the tribe of your inheritance, this Mount Zion.”
At the Red Sea: “he saved them from the hand of the hater, וַיִּגְאָלֵם from the hand of the enemy.”
“They remembered that God was their rock, and the Most High God their redeemer.”
“Do not fear, for I have redeemed you; I have called you by your name; you are mine.”
“Return to me, for I have redeemed you … Yahweh has redeemed Jacob.”
“Go out from Babylon … say, Yahweh has redeemed his servant Jacob.”
“You shall go to Babylon; there you shall be delivered, there Yahweh shall redeem you from the hand of your enemies.”
“Yahweh has ransomed (פָדָה) Jacob, and redeemed him from the hand of one stronger than he.”
“Yahweh has comforted his people, he has redeemed Jerusalem.”
“Who made the depths of the sea a way for the redeemed (גְּאוּלִים) to pass over.”
“The redeemed shall walk there.”
“They shall call them The holy people, The redeemed of Yahweh.”
“Let the redeemed of Yahweh say so, whom he redeemed from the hand of the adversary.”
“In his love and in his pity he redeemed them.”
Jacob: “the angel הַגֹּאֵל אֹתִי from all evil, bless the lads.”

senses.definition: The participle as Yahweh's name, often with “the Holy One of Israel”, “your Saviour”, “your Maker”: the God who is near kin to Israel and takes up their cause.

evidence.note: “Do not fear, worm Jacob … I help you, says Yahweh, וְגֹאֲלֵךְ the Holy One of Israel.”
“Thus says Yahweh, the King of Israel, and his redeemer, Yahweh of hosts: I am the first and I am the last, and besides me there is no God.”
“Your redeemer, and he who formed you from the womb.”
“All flesh shall know that I, Yahweh, am your Saviour (מוֹשִׁיעֵךְ) and your redeemer, the Mighty One of Jacob”; the same at Isa 60:16.
“Your Maker is your husband (בֹעֲלַיִךְ) … and your redeemer is the Holy One of Israel”: husband and kinsman, as Boaz to Ruth.
“You, Yahweh, are our father; our redeemer from of old is your name.”
“וּבָא לְצִיּוֹן גּוֹאֵל, and to those who turn from transgression in Jacob”; Paul cites it of Christ's coming (Rom 11:26).
“The deliverer (ὁ ῥυόμενος; Peshitta פָּרוֹקָא) shall come out of Zion, and turn away ungodliness from Jacob.”
“Yahweh, my rock and my redeemer.”
“Do not enter the fields of the fatherless, for their redeemer is strong; he will plead their cause against you”: the orphan has no human kinsman, and Yahweh is that kinsman.
“Their redeemer is strong; Yahweh of hosts is his name; he will surely plead their cause.”

senses.gloss: redeem a life from trouble, death, the grave
senses.definition: Of God, to take up the cause of one in trouble and bring his life back: from the pit, from death and the grave.

evidence.note: “From the hand of the grave (שְׁאוֹל) I will ransom them; from death אֶגְאָלֵם. O death, where are your plagues? O grave, where is your destruction?”
Paul takes Hos 13:14 as fulfilled when “this mortal puts on immortality” at the resurrection: “O death, where is your sting?”
“הַגּוֹאֵל מִשַּׁחַת חַיָּיְכִי”: who redeems your life from the pit.
“I know that גֹּאֲלִי חָי, and at the last he shall stand upon the dust.”
“You have pleaded the causes of my soul, Lord; you have redeemed my life.”
“Draw near to my soul, redeem it; ransom me (פְּדֵנִי) because of my enemies.”
“Plead my cause and redeem me; give me life according to your word.”

senses.definition: Of a house, a field, a servant or a dedicated thing, to be bought back; what is devoted (חֵרֶם) or exchanged may not be. Once, reflexive: to redeem oneself.

evidence.note: “If it is not redeemed within a full year, the house in the walled city shall be the buyer's for ever.”
“Or if he is able, וְנִגְאָל”: he redeems himself.
“If he is not redeemed by these, he shall go out in the year of jubilee.”
“No devoted thing … shall be sold or redeemed; every devoted thing is most holy to Yahweh.”
“You were sold for nothing, and you shall be redeemed without silver.”
“You were not redeemed with corruptible things, silver or gold … but with the precious blood of Christ”: the redemption without silver.

evidence.locator: Exo.6.6, וְגָאַלְתִּי → λυτρώσομαι; Exo.15.13; Lev.25.25; Psa.103.4; Lam.3.58; Hos.13.14 → λυτρόω; Isa.52.3 → λυτρωθήσεσθε; λυτρόω renders גָּאַל ×25

evidence.note: “We hoped that it was he who was about to redeem (λυτροῦσθαι) Israel.”
“Who gave himself for us, that he might redeem (λυτρώσηται) us from all lawlessness.”
“You were redeemed (ἐλυτρώθητε) not with silver or gold”, as Isa 52:3.

evidence.locator: Isa.44.6, גֹּאֲלוֹ → ῥυσάμενος; ῥύομαι renders גָּאַל ×5

evidence.note: Isa 59:20 quoted: “ἥξει ἐκ Σιὼν ὁ ῥυόμενος”, the redeemer who comes to Zion.
Moses, whom Israel refused, “God sent as ruler and redeemer (λυτρωτήν)”.

parallels.note: “Ransom”, set beside גָּאַל of the same deliverance.
“Save”: Yahweh is Israel's Saviour and Redeemer.
“Plead a cause”: the kinsman takes up the cause of the one he redeems.
“Near”: the גֹּאֵל is the near kinsman.

phrases.gloss: your Redeemer, the Holy One of Israel

words.gloss: redemption; right of redemption; redemption price; kindred
words.summary: Fourteen times, in the law of the jubilee, in Ruth and Jeremiah's purchase of his cousin's field, and once in Ezekiel, where “the men of your גְּאֻלָּה” are the kindred whose land it is to redeem.

senses.definition: The buying back of land or a man sold, and the right to do it, which belongs to the near kinsman and lasts until the jubilee, or a year for a house in a walled city.

evidence.note: “In all the land of your possession you shall grant גְּאֻלָּה for the land”, because “the land is mine” (Lev 25:23).
A house in a walled city: “its redemption shall be until a full year after it is sold.”
“The Levites shall have redemption for ever.”
“After he is sold, גְּאֻלָּה shall be his.”
Hanamel to Jeremiah: “Buy my field in Anathoth, for the right of redemption (מִשְׁפַּט הַגְּאֻלָּה) is yours to buy it.”
“For the right of inheritance is yours, and the redemption is yours.”
“Redeem my redemption (גְּאֻלָּתִי) for yourself”: the nearer kinsman gives up his right to Boaz.
“This was the custom in former time in Israel concerning redemption and exchange”: the shoe drawn off.

senses.definition: What must be paid to buy back a man or a field, reckoned by the years left until the jubilee.

evidence.note: “He himself becomes able and finds enough for his redemption.”
“According to them he shall give back the price of his redemption … according to his years he shall give back his redemption.”

senses.gloss: kindred, those with the right of redemption
senses.definition: The men whose kinship gives them the right to redeem: in Ezekiel, the exiles, Ezekiel's own brothers, to whom the land of Israel will be given again.

evidence.note: “Your brothers, your brothers, אַנְשֵׁי גְאֻלָּתֶךָ, and all the house of Israel”, of whom Jerusalem's people said, “to us the land is given”.
“I will gather you from the peoples … and I will give you the land of Israel.”
Anna spoke of the child “to all who looked for redemption (λύτρωσιν) in Jerusalem”.
“He has visited and wrought redemption (λύτρωσιν) for his people.”

words.summary: Once, Isa 63:4 שְׁנַת גְּאוּלַי, “the year of my redemption” (or “of my redeemed”, if it is the plural passive participle of the verb, as in Isa 35:9). One use: the form, not the meaning, is in doubt. The brief files the verb's tokens under this key as well, so its count is the verb's.

senses.definition: The redeeming of Yahweh's people, set beside the day of vengeance on their enemies.

evidence.note: “For the day of vengeance (יוֹם נָקָם) was in my heart, and the year of my redemption (וּשְׁנַת גְּאוּלַי) has come.”
The same pair: “to proclaim the year of Yahweh's favour and the day of vengeance of our God.”

words.gloss: defile, stain, pollute; (pual) be defiled, be put out as unclean
words.summary: Eleven times (twelve with Job 3:5), almost all in late books: hands and garments stained with blood, bread polluted on the altar, Daniel refusing to defile himself with the king's food, priests without a genealogy put out of the priesthood as defiled. No cognate has been found for it, and its link to גָּאַל “redeem” is not understood; it may be another older root in the same spelling, or a by-form of גָּעַל “loathe”. Blood is common to both verbs (the avenger of blood; hands stained with blood), but the verses do not join them.

senses.definition: Of darkness covering a day as a stain: Job curses the day of his birth.

evidence.note: “יִגְאָלֻהוּ חֹשֶׁךְ וְצַלְמָוֶת; let a cloud dwell upon it; let the blackness of the day terrify it.” The parallels are covering and terror. Read with the first verb, it is “let darkness claim it”.

senses.definition: Of hands, of men and of a city: to be stained with blood or polluted by sin.

evidence.note: “Your hands נְגֹאֲלוּ בַדָּם, and your fingers with iniquity.”
The prophets and priests who shed the blood of the righteous “wandered blind in the streets; they were defiled with blood, so that none could touch their garments.”
“Woe to her that is rebellious וְנִגְאָלָה, the oppressing city.”

senses.definition: To treat as unclean what belongs to Yahweh, by offering what is despised at his table.

evidence.note: “You offer לֶחֶם מְגֹאָל on my altar, and you say, בַּמֶּה גֵאַלְנוּךָ? In that you say, The table of Yahweh is despised.”

stems.gloss: be defiled; be put out as defiled

senses.definition: The participle: the bread and the table of Yahweh made unclean by blemished offerings.

evidence.note: “You profane (מְחַלְּלִים) it, in that you say, The table of the Lord is מְגֹאָל, and its fruit, its food, is despised.”
What made it so: “When you offer the blind … the lame and sick, is it not evil?”

senses.gloss: be put out of the priesthood as unclean
senses.definition: Of men claiming to be priests who could not show their genealogy: they were treated as unclean and removed.

evidence.note: “These sought their register … but they were not found; וַיְגֹאֲלוּ מִן־הַכְּהֻנָּה.” They were not to eat of the most holy things until a priest stood up with Urim and Thummim (Ezr 2:63).

senses.definition: Of the one who treads the winepress of the nations: their blood spattered on his garments and stained them.

evidence.note: “Their juice is sprinkled on my garments, וְכָל־מַלְבּוּשַׁי אֶגְאָלְתִּי”, in the day of vengeance and the year of redemption (Isa 63:4).
“Who is this who comes from Edom, with garments dyed red from Bozrah?”
“Clothed with a garment dipped in blood … and he treads the winepress of the fierceness of the wrath of God Almighty.”

senses.definition: To make oneself unclean by eating what the law forbids or what was offered to idols.

evidence.note: “Daniel set upon his heart אֲשֶׁר לֹא־יִתְגָּאַל with the king's portion of food or with the wine he drank.”
“That they abstain from the pollutions (ἀλισγημάτων) of idols”: the noun of the Septuagint's verb for Mal 1:7.
“A few names in Sardis who have not defiled (ἐμόλυναν) their garments”, against the priests of Lam 4:14 whose garments none could touch.
Food offered to an idol: “their conscience, being weak, is defiled (μολύνεται)”, as Daniel would not defile himself.

parallels.note: “Profane”: the table defiled is the table profaned.
“Despise”: the defiled bread is what is despised.

words.summary: Once, in the plural: the defiling of the priesthood by a priest's son who married a foreign wife.

senses.definition: What makes the priesthood unclean: here, the high priest's grandson married to the daughter of Sanballat.

evidence.note: “Remember them, my God, עַל גָּאֳלֵי הַכְּהֻנָּה, and the covenant of the priesthood and of the Levites.”
The cause: “one of the sons of Joiada, son of Eliashib the high priest, was son-in-law to Sanballat the Horonite.”

cognates.note: Jewish Aramaic, in the Targum of Onkelos for the Hebrew גֹּאֵל הַדָּם of Num 35. It is the Hebrew term carried over: the Targums' own word for redeem and redeemer is פְּרַק, פָּרוֹקָא (Targ. Ruth 4:3), as the Peshitta's is ܦܪܩ (Rom 11:26). Not independent evidence of the Hebrew's meaning.

evidence.locator: s.v. גְּאַל (ch.), part. גָּאֵל, גָּאֵיל, citing Targ. O. Num. XXXV, 12; 19; 21 (ג׳ דמא)
s.v. פָּרוֹקָא, citing Targ. Ruth IV, 3; Targ. Y. Ex. XV, 18
evidence.note: redeemer

cognates.gloss: wages, pay; pay given to one who goes to war as a substitute
cognates.note: Offered as a cognate of גָּאַל through the verb جَعَلَ “make, set”, but Arabic ʿ does not answer Hebrew א, and the sense touches redemption only in the payment for a substitute. A lead, not evidence.

evidence.locator: Book I, p. 431, art. جعل, جُعْلٌ (n5930)
evidence.note: “Wages; pay; a stipend … wages, or pay, which one gives to a man who goes to war as a substitute for the giver.”
“Possibly connected to Arabic جَعَلَ (jaʕala, ‘to fix, to set’).”

doctrine.statement: The law gave the right and duty to redeem to the near kinsman, “his redeemer who is near to him”, a brother, an uncle, “any of the remnant of his flesh, of his family” (Lev 25:25, 48–49); a stranger could not act, and a nearer kinsman came first (Rut 3:12; 4:4–6). Yahweh calls himself Israel's גֹּאֵל and husband (Isa 54:5), and promises “a redeemer shall come to Zion, and to those who turn from transgression in Jacob” (Isa 59:20); Paul applies the verse to Jesus (Rom 11:26–27). The New Testament shows him a kinsman in flesh: “God sent forth his Son, born of a woman, born under the law, to redeem those under the law” (Gal 4:4–5); “since the children share in flesh and blood, he himself likewise partook of the same, that through death he might destroy him who had the power of death, that is, the false accuser” (Heb 2:14), and “it was necessary for him to be made like his brothers in all things” (Heb 2:17). Israel was “sold for nothing” and was to be redeemed “without silver” (Isa 52:3), and Peter says they were redeemed “not with silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ” (1Pe 1:18–19). From the verses: the redeemer had to be of the family he redeemed; God provided his Son as a man of our flesh and blood, a true kinsman, who by his own death bought back those who could not redeem themselves.

Job asked, “If a man dies, shall he live again? All the days of my service I will wait until my change comes” (Job 14:14), and answered, “I know that my redeemer lives, and at the last he shall stand upon the dust; and after my skin is destroyed, this, yet from my flesh I shall see God” (Job 19:25–26): the kinsman who takes up his cause stands on the earth at the last, and Job sees God in his flesh, after death and not at it. Yahweh says, “From the hand of the grave I will ransom them; from death I will redeem them. O death, where are your plagues? O grave, where is your destruction?” (Hos 13:14), and Paul quotes it of the moment when “the dead shall be raised incorruptible” at the last trumpet and “this mortal shall put on immortality” (1Co 15:52–55). Those who have the firstfruits of the spirit wait for “the redemption of our body” (Rom 8:23), and the Lord himself will descend and “the dead in Christ shall rise” (1Th 4:16). From the verses: redemption from death is the raising of the body from the dust when the redeemer stands on the earth at Christ's return; man is mortal until then, and the hope is not an immortal soul at death but a body raised to life.

“The land shall not be sold for ever, for the land is mine; you are strangers and sojourners with me. In all the land of your possession you shall grant redemption for the land” (Lev 25:23–24): the land of Israel is Yahweh's, held by families who may lose it for a time but not for ever. While Jerusalem was besieged Jeremiah bought his cousin's field “because the right of redemption is yours”, as a sign that “houses and fields and vineyards shall again be bought in this land” (Jer 32:7–8, 15, 44). To the exiles, “the men of your redemption”, whom Jerusalem's people said were far from Yahweh, he answered, “I will gather you from the peoples … and I will give you the land of Israel” (Ezk 11:15–17). From the verses: Yahweh is the kinsman who will buy back his land for his people, and its return to them is part of the redemption the prophets promised.

The one who comes from Edom with garments stained red treads the winepress alone: “their juice is sprinkled on my garments, and I have stained (אֶגְאָלְתִּי) all my clothing; for the day of vengeance was in my heart, and the year of my redemption has come” (Isa 63:1–4). The avenger of blood and the redeemer are the same kinsman (Num 35:19; Lev 25:25). Jesus read Isa 61:1–2 in Nazareth and stopped at “the acceptable year of the Lord”, before “the day of vengeance of our God” (Luk 4:18–21; Isa 61:2), and John sees him come from heaven “clothed with a garment dipped in blood … and he treads the winepress of the fierceness of the wrath of God” (Rev 19:13–15). From the verses: the redeemer who buys back his people also avenges them, and that day of vengeance is at his coming.

note: Drafted 2026-11-19. Root key גאל; no existing entry used it. BDB keys: c.ac.aa the verb redeem; c.ac.ac גְּאֻלָּה; c.ac.ab גְּאוּלִים (Isa 63:4; the database files all the verb's tokens under this key too, so its count is the verb's); c.ad.aa the verb defile; c.ad.ab גֹּאֶל; c.ac.ad the name Igal (names/igal.json). j.aj.af (יִגְאָל, a zero-token verb cross-reference “see גאל”) is left unassigned. One entry for both verbs, as one spelling one entry; they share no cognate and the verses do not link them. Job 3:5 (יִגְאָלֻהוּ) is tagged with the redeem verb in the data but placed here under the defile verb's qal, since its parallels are cloud and blackness covering the day; the Targum of Job renders it with a verb “moisten” (variant “defile”, Jastrow s.v. טְנַן). The other reading, “let darkness claim it” as a kinsman claims, is possible; open question. The defile verb may be a by-form of גָּעַל “loathe” (Lev 26:11; Ezk 16:5), not a cognate; not followed. Cognates: none secure. Jewish Aramaic גְּאַל is a Hebraism (the Targums use פְּרַק), named on the verb and גְּאֻלָּה because it shares their meaning, though lexicon-support then counts it as support it is not; Arabic جُعْل is a weak lead (ʿ for א). Leads not followed: Ugaritic (DULAT not vendored), Amorite personal names, Old South Arabian. The Peshitta has no cognate root (redeem is ܦܪܩ). Greek ἀγχιστεύς/ἀγχιστεύω (Ruth; Ezr 2:62 for the defile verb, the translator reading it as the redeem verb) has no New Testament use and is not recorded. Open questions: (1) Job 3:5, which verb; (2) whether גְּאוּלַי is a noun or the passive participle. The doctrine statements are reasoned conclusions to review.
